extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners and parties in PTAB inter partes review proceedings (petitioners, patent owners, counsel, expert witnesses)
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and procedural/legal criteria used by the Patent Trial and Appeal Board when deciding whether to institute an inter partes review and how to analyze asserted obviousness grounds under 35 U.S.C. § 103. Includes burden rules, claim construction standards, level-of-skill factors, and obviousness combination reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Petitioner burden to identify unpatentability with particularity
rubrics_metrics.description: “In an [inter partes review], the petitioner has the burden from the onset to show with particularity why the patent it challenges is unpatentable.” (citing Harmonic Inc. v. Avid Tech., Inc.; 35 U.S.C. § 312(a)(3)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Petition must identify with particularity the evidence that supports the grounds for the challenge to each claim. The petition should map claim limitations to prior art and present supporting evidence (e.g., declarations, alignments). Failure to identify evidence with particularity can defeat institution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of persuasion remains on petitioner
rubrics_metrics.description: “This burden of persuasion never shifts to the patent owner.” (citing Dynamic Drinkware, LLC v. Nat’l Graphics, Inc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even in preliminaries (institution stage), petitioner must carry the burden of persuasion to show a reasonable likelihood of prevailing; patent owner is not required to prove patentability at institution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obviousness standard under 35 U.S.C. § 103 (Graham factors)
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim is unpatentable under 35 U.S.C. § 103(a) if the differences between the claimed subject matter and the prior art are such that the subject matter as a whole would have been obvious to a person having ordinary skill in the art. The question is resolved by underlying factual determinations including: (1) scope and content of the prior art; (2) differences between the claimed subject matter and the prior art; (3) level of ordinary skill in the art; and (4) objective evidence of nonobviousness, if any. (Graham v. John Deere Co.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Obviousness analyses must address each Graham factor; show where each claim limitation is taught or suggested by prior art and explain the differences and why a POSA would have been motivated to bridge them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motivation to combine and reasonable expectation of success
rubrics_metrics.description: To show obviousness of a combination of prior art elements, a party must show that a skilled artisan would have been motivated to combine the teachings of the prior art to achieve the claimed invention and would have had a reasonable expectation of success. (KSR, In re Magnum Oil Tools).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both the suggestion/motivation and the expectation of success must be grounded in the prior art, not applicant disclosure (In re Dow Chemical). Evidence (experimental data, teachings, known problems) should be provided to show why a POSA would combine references and expect success.

rubrics_metrics.name: KSR guidance on 'obvious to try' and predictability
rubrics_metrics.description: KSR instructs that when there is a design need or market pressure and a finite number of identified, predictable solutions, it may be obvious to try known options — and success following predictable options can indicate obviousness. KSR also states that an improvement is barred from patentability if it is merely the predictable use of prior art elements according to their established functions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain why the combination falls within a ‘finite, predictable’ set of solutions or why the claimed improvement is more than predictable use. Show why a POSA would pursue the known option(s) rather than relying on hindsight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim construction standard in IPR
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims in an IPR are construed using the same standard as in a civil action under 35 U.S.C. § 282(b): in accordance with the ordinary and customary meaning to one of ordinary skill in the art and the prosecution history. The specification is highly relevant and usually dispositive. (37 C.F.R. § 42.100(b); Phillips; In re Abbott Diabetes Care).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board will construe only those terms that are in controversy and only to the extent necessary to resolve the controversy (Realtime Data; Vivid Techs.). If claim terms are not disputed for institution purposes, express constructions may be unnecessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determining level of ordinary skill in the art (POSA)
rubrics_metrics.description: Factors include the type of problems encountered in the art, prior art solutions to those problems, the rapidity with which innovations are made, the sophistication of the technology, and the educational level of active workers in the field. (Custom Accessories; Orthopedic Equip.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Petitioners/patent owners should articulate and support a POSA definition (e.g., degrees, years experience) and tie that definition to the prior art and specification; the Board may accept an uncontested POSA definition for institution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mapping claim limitations to the prior art with supporting evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: To meet the petitioner's burden at institution, the petition must show that each limitation of a challenged claim is taught or rendered obvious by the asserted references, using factual evidence (e.g., reference paragraphs, sequence alignments, expert declarations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide explicit citations and demonstrative evidence (sequence alignments, tables, experiment results, expert testimony) that show how each claim limitation is present in or suggested by the prior art; courts/Board expect concrete linkages rather than conclusory assertions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expert declarations and unrebutted testimony as evidentiary support
rubrics_metrics.description: Testimony from experts (declarations) about sequence alignments, routine experimentation, POSA understanding, and use of analysis tools can support the petitioner's showing; unrebutted testimony at institution stage may be credited by the Board.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include clear explanation of methods (e.g., Clustal parameters), reproducible alignments, and expert reasoning; anticipate and address potential patent-owner rebuttals to avoid being credited as 'unrebutted' improperly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain selection and focus among multiple prior-art alternatives
rubrics_metrics.description: When a reference discloses many possible embodiments or dozens of sequences, the petitioner must explain why a POSA would have selected the particular reference or embodiment as a starting point for modification (i.e., why that choice is not hindsight).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show teachings in the prior art that highlight the chosen reference's promise (examples, experimental data, express comparisons) or otherwise provide a reasoned motivation for selecting it over alternative disclosures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show why a particular modification would have been made (choice of specific changes)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is insufficient to show only that two sequences differ; to establish obviousness over a reference combination, the petitioner should explain why a POSA would have made the specific substitution(s) (e.g., a particular amino acid change) rather than other changes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide prior-art teachings (e.g., mechanism-based reasoning such as phosphorylation site removal), predictive tools, or experimental data that would have led a POSA to make the specific modification with a reasonable expectation of success.

rubrics_metrics.name: When combining references, address claim-specific functional/limitation requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: If a claim requires a specific function or tropism (e.g., muscle tropism for claim 8), the petitioner must explain why the combined teachings would yield that particular functional property, not just some general improvement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrate that the asserted combination would provide the claimed function (e.g., cite data showing muscle transduction or explain why the modification specifically enhances muscle targeting), or identify where the prior art links the modification to the required function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institution decision standard: reasonable likelihood of prevailing
rubrics_metrics.description: Under 35 U.S.C. § 314(a) the Board institutes review if the petitioner shows a reasonable likelihood that it would prevail with respect to at least one of the claims challenged. The Board applies SAS and relevant rules (37 C.F.R. § 42.108(a)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Petition should present the strongest grounds with coherent evidence and argumentation. The Board may focus its institution analysis on the strongest ground(s) and limit its discussion accordingly; institution is not a final determination of patentability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of specification and prosecution history as primary guides for claim meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification is the single best guide to the meaning of a disputed claim term and prosecution history is relevant to claim construction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When interpreting claim terms or arguing what a POSA would have understood, rely on the patent's specification and prosecution history to frame meanings and limits; avoid constructions contrary to the specification unless clearly supported.
